source.title: Magic matrices with their powers, numerical ranges and some open problems

accepted.question_text: Let a magic matrix of order n mean an n by n square matrix whose entries are the natural numbers 1, 2, ..., n^2 with no repeated entry, and whose row sums, column sums, main diagonal sum, and antidiagonal sum are all equal. For general n, how can one describe exactly, or estimate, the number of magic matrices of order n?

evidence.quote: square matrices (of order n) satisfying the following conditions: (m1) the entries aij of A belong to the set {1, 2, . . . , n2 }, (m2) if (i, j) 6= (k, l) then aij 6= akl , (m3) the sums in each row, each column, main diagonal and antidiagonal are equal.
Open problem 1. Describe or estimate the number of magic matrices of order n (for small values of n some results are known).

accepted.question_text: Let a magic matrix of order n mean an n by n square matrix whose entries are the natural numbers 1, 2, ..., n^2 with no repeated entry, and whose row sums, column sums, main diagonal sum, and antidiagonal sum are all equal. Is it true in general that magic matrices of odd order have full rank, whereas magic matrices of even order have rank strictly smaller than their order?

evidence.quote: square matrices (of order n) satisfying the following conditions: (m1) the entries aij of A belong to the set {1, 2, . . . , n2 }, (m2) if (i, j) 6= (k, l) then aij 6= akl , (m3) the sums in each row, each column, main diagonal and antidiagonal are equal.
Open problem 2. Magic matrices of odd order seem to be of full rank, while magic matrices of even order seem to have rank strictly smaller than their order. Is that true in general?

accepted.question_text: Let a magic matrix of order n mean an n by n square matrix whose entries are the natural numbers 1, 2, ..., n^2 with no repeated entry, and whose row sums, column sums, main diagonal sum, and antidiagonal sum are all equal. For any such matrix, let s denote the common row, column, main diagonal, and antidiagonal sum, which is an eigenvalue. Among magic matrices of the same order, how much can the eigenvalues other than s differ? May those non-s eigenvalues have arbitrary phase, and are they always symmetric with respect to zero?

evidence.quote: square matrices (of order n) satisfying the following conditions: (m1) the entries aij of A belong to the set {1, 2, . . . , n2 }, (m2) if (i, j) 6= (k, l) then aij 6= akl , (m3) the sums in each row, each column, main diagonal and antidiagonal are equal.
From now on s will denote this number. We easily verify that s is an eigenvalue of the magic matrix and a corresponding eigenvector is x = (1, 1, . . . , 1)T .

Open problem 3. The magic matrices exhibited in Remark 1.1 and Remark 2.1 have different eigenvalues (apart from s) than matrices of the same order generated by MATLAB. How much may the eigenvalues of different magic matrices of the same order differ? May they have an arbitrary phase? Are they always symmetric with respect to zero (not counting s)?
